official_authority.interpretation: 5.1 permits result-unrelated changes;5.2/5.3 require eligiblealternatives AND likelyresult-basedselection. Source dates/mismatch/multiplicity alone do not establish it.

findings.classification: defensible unresolved chronology, not uniquely required NI
findings.assessment: The cited draft date follows reported follow-up completion. Neither event establishes unblinded access. NI is defensible, but exact timestamps are not required for ProbablyYes. The 2015 protocol already specifies assignment-group mixed models, random intercepts and blinded-statistician intent; this is supportive earlier planning, not proof that blinding/timing safeguards were carried out. Original covariate and timing descriptions differ in detail from the later SAP. A qualified probably judgment can be defensible if that consistency and trial circumstances support it; no operator answer imposed.
findings.citation_issue: The report follow-up completion date is read in mainpage1 but absent from the5.1 cited bases. It is a source-supported fact, not a fabricated date; the durable warrant does not bind that chronology premise to its actual passage.
findings.under_discussed: Cited supplement1page1 also documents an early amendment for repeated-measures power error. This stated result-unrelated rationale should be considered separately from late SAP timing, without treating either as proof of access chronology.

findings.assessment: Main Table2 fully reports 18,26,52week pain estimates including a nonsignificant52week estimate. This supports a reassuring conclusion for the later stated schedule. However the unread original protocolpage4 specified baseline,3/6weeks during treatment,immediatepost-treatment and laterpost-treatment assessments. The saved No warrant does not reconcile those earlier intended measurements or qualify their applicability. The discrepancy alone does not show eligible alternatives were measured, withheld, or selected on results; it does not warrant automatic Yes/ProbablyYes. A probably-no inference or unresolved qualification may be more defensible than categorical all-intentions correspondence.
findings.citation_issue: Bases cite SAPprimarydefinition and mainanalysis methods only; actual Table2/Table3 reporting asserted in prose is not in this question’s selected bases, though it was read and Table2was available as Evidence.

findings.classification: generally reassuring matching primary method; incomplete citation/qualification
findings.assessment: SAP13 and report4 both specify assignment-group mixed models and the18weekcontrast. The fullanalysisset and MAR/no-imputation statement is retained in the exact Result; the separate principal-complier analysis is not silently substituted for it. Reporting a primary and complier analysis is not evidence of result-driven selection. Original2015modelprognosticcovariates and laterSAP14plannedpossibleATET, plus eight-versus-nine-session compliance definitions, deserve qualified handling: their eligibility for this assignment-effect Result is not established. No unsupported selective-reporting defect is inferred.
findings.citation_issue: The warrant says the complier estimate is reported, but its bases contain SAPprimarymodel, mainanalysisdescription and Table2primary/secondaryoutcomes; the actual complierestimate is in main8, which was read but not cited. Do not substitute methods for actual result disclosure.

Primary outcome
We will use a mixed-effects model to estimate the effect of allocation to intervention group on the primary
outcome; pain intensity at 18-weeks post randomisation. Mixed-effect models are recommended for
estimating treatment effects at specific time-points in clinical trials.54256 We will model intervention group
as a binary variable and time as a categorical variable with 4 levels corresponding to the repeated measures.
We will use an unconstrained correlation structure as this is most plausible, given the repeated
measurements are at different time intervals. The model will include three fixed-effect terms for the
group.time interactions and a random intercept. The intercept term will account for the dependency of
observations within participants due to repeated measures. The model is

bases.stopping_rationale: I inspected the supplement's protocol chronology (page 1), SAP content and date (pages 7, 12-13), and the main report's follow-up and analysis sections. These establish SAP drafting after follow-up completion and the reported analysis, but not investigator access timing; no captured source passage resolves that missing event.
bases.unresolved_premise: The captured sources do not report when investigators making analysis decisions first accessed unblinded outcome data.

exact_warrants.justification: The captured supplement dates the SAP draft to March 2, 2020, and describes the approved primary endpoint/analysis as pain intensity at 18 weeks using a mixed-effects model. The main report says follow-up was completed February 3, 2020, and reports the corresponding 18-week analysis. However, neither source establishes when unblinded outcome data became available to the investigators making analysis decisions. The chronology raises a concern that the SAP was drafted after outcome collection, but collection completion, data cutoff, or a draft date alone does not establish investigator access. Under the question's uncertainty rule, neither a definitive nor probable timing judgment is sufficiently grounded.
unknowns: When investigators first had access to unblinded outcome data; whether the March 2, 2020 SAP draft was finalized before such access.

exact_warrants.justification: The SAP identifies one primary pain measurement: average pain intensity in the previous week on a subject-rated 0-10 NRS at 18 weeks. The report provides pain results at the specified primary time point and also reports follow-up pain at 26 and 52 weeks. It separately identifies recovery and response thresholds as post hoc outcomes and reports both 30% and 50% response definitions. Thus the inspected material does not show an eligible pain measurement selected from multiple eligible scales/definitions with only a favorable subset reported; the stated primary measure and the presented additional pain follow-ups/threshold results are reported.

The report also discloses a separately specified complier causal-effect analysis and reports its estimate. The captured passages do not identify a set of eligible alternative analyses from which the 18-week primary estimate was selected based on results, nor a result-driven reporting choice. Although the SAP's chronology relative to unblinded access remains unknown, that uncertainty alone is not evidence of selection among analyses.

1|Effect of Graded Sensorimotor Retraining on Pain Intensity
2|in Patients With Chronic Low Back Pain
3|A Randomized Clinical Trial
4|Matthew K. Bagg, PhD; Benedict M. Wand, PhD; Aidan G. Cashin, PhD; Hopin Lee, PhD; Markus Hübscher, PhD;
5|Tasha R. Stanton, PhD; Neil E. O'Connell, PhD; Edel T. O'Hagan, MSc; Rodrigo R. N. Rizzo, MSc; Michael A. Wewege, MSc;
6|Martin Rabey, PhD; Stephen Goodall, PhD; Sopany Saing, MPH; Serigne N. Lo, PhD; Hannu Luomajoki, PhD;
7|Robert D. Herbert, PhD; Chris G. Maher, DMedSc; G. Lorimer Moseley, PhD; James H. McAuley, PhD
8|IMPORTANCE The effects of altered neural processing, defined as altering neural networks
9|responsible for perceptions of pain and function, on chronic pain remains unclear.
10|OBJECTIVE To estimate the effect of a graded sensorimotor retraining intervention
11|(RESOLVE) on pain intensity in people with chronic low back pain.
12|DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This parallel, 2-group, randomized clinical trial recruited
13|participants with chronic (>3 months) nonspecific low back pain from primary care and
14|community settings. A total of 276 adults were randomized (in a 1:1 ratio) to the intervention
15|or sham procedure and attention control groups delivered by clinicians at a medical research
16|institute in Sydney, Australia. The first participant was randomized on December 10, 2015,
17|and the last was randomized on July 25, 2019. Follow-up was completed on February 3, 2020.
18|INTERVENTIONS Participants randomized to the intervention group (n = 138) were asked to
19|participate in 12 weekly clinical sessions and home training designed to educate them about
20|and assist them with movement and physical activity while experiencing lower back pain.
21|Participants randomized to the control group (n = 138) were asked to participate in 12 weekly
22|clinical sessions and home training that required similar time as the intervention but did not
23|focus on education, movement, and physical activity. The control group included sham laser
24|and shortwave diathermy applied to the back and sham noninvasive brain stimulation.
25|MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES The primary outcome was pain intensity at 18 weeks,
26|measured on an 11-point numerical rating scale (range, 0 [no pain] to 10 [worst pain
27|imaginable]) for which the between-group minimum clinically important difference
28|is 1.0 point.
29|RESULTS Among 276 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 46 [14.3] years; 138 [50%]
30|women), 261 (95%) completed follow-up at 18 weeks. The mean pain intensity was 5.6 at
31|baseline and 3.1 at 18 weeks in the intervention group and 5.8 at baseline and 4.0 at 18 weeks
32|in the control group, with an estimated between-group mean difference at 18 weeks
33|of -1.0 point ([95% CI, -1.5 to -0.4]; P = .001), favoring the intervention group.
34|CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this randomized clinical trial conducted at a single center
35|among patients with chronic low back pain, graded sensorimotor retraining, compared with a
36|sham procedure and attention control, significantly improved pain intensity at 18 weeks. The
37|improvements in pain intensity were small, and further research is needed to understand the
38|generalizability of the findings.

32|Data were collected at baseline (prior to randomization) and

92|Post hoc outcomes consisted of recovery, defined as pain in-

94|11-point numerical rating scale at both 18 and 26 weeks after

96|tion, defined as at least 30% reduction in pain intensity from
97|baseline to 18 weeks; response to intervention, defined as at
98|least50%reductioninpainintensityfrombaselineto18weeks;
99|and global perceived effect, assessed using the Global Back
100|Recovery Scale (range, -5 to 5; lower scores indicate poorer re-
101|covery; MCID not established).

25|Blinding
26|Patients will be blinded to group allocation and study hypothesis. It is not possible for therapists to be blinded to the
27|study hypothesis as the treating therapists are on the research team. The statistician analysing the data will be blind to
28|group allocation.
29|
30|Sample Size Calculations
31|We require 266 patients to detect a one point (SD=2.5) between group difference in the first primary outcome, pain
32|intensity (Numerical Rating Scale), at six weeks post intervention. We consider this to be the smallest worthwhile effects
33|that would justify implementation of the intervention. A one point on the NRS is established as the minimal clinically
34|important difference for pain intensity in chronic pain clinical trials (Dworkin et al., 2008).
35|Sample size was calculated using the Glimmpse software. We calculated for 7 repeated observations, an estimated
36|intra-cluster correlation (correlation between the observations) with base 0.6 and decay rate 0.1, Type I error (alpha)
37|of 5% and allowing for up to 15% loss to follow up. We conservatively ignored the increase in statistical power conferred
38|by baseline covariates and stratification.
39|
40|Outcomes
41|The primary outcomes will be pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale) and Disability (Roland Morris Disability
42|Questionnaire) at six weeks post intervention.
43|Secondary outcomes will include two-point discrimination distance, left-right recognition accuracy, depression subscale
44|of the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21), Pain Catastrophising Scale, credibility and expectancy
45|questionnaire, Neurophysiology of Pain questionnaire, Back Beliefs Questionnaire, Fremantle Back Awareness
46|Questionnaire, Tampa Scale of Kinesophobia, Pain Self-Efficacy Questionnaire, Insomnia Severity Index, EuroQoL 5D-5L,
47|Movement Imagery Questionnaire-Revised, Health Resource Use and Usual Activities, Elgueta-Cancino Pelvic Tilt Test.
48|A measure of recurrence will be taken at 52 weeks for patients who are pain free for a month or longer.
49|Participants will be assessed in all measures at baseline, 3 and 6 weeks of the intervention, immediately post-
50|intervention (week 12) and at 6 weeks, 3, 6 and 12 months post-intervention. All questionnaires will be accessible via
51|secure web-links emailed to patients individually. Tactile acuity will be assessed using two-point discrimination by the
52|study therapists. The Recognise® software provides left-right recognition accuracy and response time data. Individual
53|participant data will be extracted into a spreadsheet using software.

5|Statistical Analysis
6|The data will be analysed by intention-to-treat by a statistician blinded to group allocation. We will analyse the effect
7|of the treatment intervention separately for each outcome using linear mixed models with random intercepts for
8|individuals to account for correlation of repeated measures. The model will include terms for important prognostic
9|factors measured prior to randomisation and specified a priori. We will obtain estimates of the effect of the intervention
10|and 95% confidence intervals by constructing linear contrasts to compare the adjusted mean change (continuous
11|variables) or difference in proportions (dichotomous variables) in outcome from baseline to each time point between
12|the treatment and control group. Linear contrasts will be used to determine the effect of Informed Sensorimotor
13|Retraining compared to placebo control.

5|Analytic Principles
6|General considerations
7|We will conduct the analyses respecting these principles:
8|* all participants will be analysed in the group to which they were allocated (intention-to-treat39)
9|* all treatment effect estimates will be provided along with their associated 95% confidence intervals
10|* all statistical tests will be 2-sided with a nominal alpha level of .05
11|* P values will not be adjusted for multiplicity. However, the outcomes are clearly categorised by
12|degree of importance33 and no subgroup analysis will be performed.
13|* the null hypothesis for each outcome is that there is no difference between the intervention groups.
14|Whereas, the alternative hypothesis is that graded sensory-motor precision training is superior to the
15|control intervention.
16|* all analyses will be performed using STATA40 and R.41243
17|Outcome definitions
18|Primary outcome:
19|The primary outcome is pain intensity, defined as average pain intensity in the past week, assessed using a
20|subject-rated 11-point NRS at 18-weeks post-randomisation.33 The numeric rating scale is a continuous
21|measure that ranges from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable).44

decision.keep: Keep the compact optional source-bound capture supported by neutral native tests: it reuses one existing basis field and WorkingNote representation, removes coordinate/checkpoint copying, and leaves ordinary citations unchanged. decision.remove: Do not retain the obsolete mandatory-seeming manual checkpoint ceremony as the preferred path; f7 already removed it. No additional ledger/tool/dimension or automatic scope inference is added. No further scope scaffolding expansion is justified.
decision.legacy: All legacy fields/serialization remain; no runtime validator/label or savedjudgment change.
decision.research_limit: Repeated absence of feature use must be reported; exclude the field from any demonstrated scientific-gain claim. Future natural-use evidence requires separate authorization.
